our mission

OUR MISSION

Robotics is the biggest step change in human history.

For many years, human lives were similar. The last 100 years have been the steepest change in human history: cars, planes, the internet, and now AI. We believe robotics will be the peak of this step change. A transformational technology that will shape lives for centuries.

Today, robotics has a 40-99 problem. Robotics companies are building bigger and more generalizable models. But ultimately, even the best models have a success rate of 40%. We are bridging the gap from 40 to 99. Only then will robotics reach widespread adoption.

There is no better way to train robots than through humans. Our team has spent the majority of our lives building robots, and it formed this core belief. We have evolutionary knowledge of the physical world, and are a far better resource for teaching robots than any tool imaginable.

Robotics has long been a promise. We are making it a reality.

How does GovGuard automate FOIA requests?
+

Our system connects securely to your city's archives. When a request comes in, our agents pinpoint relevant documents, auto-redact sensitive information, and draft the response letter for city staff.

Is my city's data secure?
+

Yes. GovGuard is built with enterprise-grade security standards. We encrypt all data at rest and in transit, and strictly isolate organization data. We are committed to maintaining the highest standards of data privacy for municipalities and are working towards SOC2 certification.

Can we customize response letters?
+

Yes. GovGuard drafts each response letter using your jurisdiction's templates and tone, and city staff can edit any draft before it goes out. Every citation and exemption is included automatically, so the letter is ready for review.

What data sources do you ingest?
+

We ingest a wide variety of file types including emails, PDFs, documents, and spreadsheets. These are pulled seamlessly from standard municipal platforms including Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, YouTube, Zoom, etc.

Today, we introduce Discovered Materials: we build AI agents that discover new materials for semiconductor chips. Alongside this, we also open-source Material Discovery Bench, a benchmark we built to measure exactly this capability.

We are backed by a $9M seed round led by Lightspeed, with participation from Y Combinator and Peak XV, and angels like Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram and Thariq Shihipar.

Intelligence has a heat problem

AI chips have a major heat problem. GPUs today handle heat fluxes of ~140 W/cm², higher than a space shuttle nose cone re-entering the earth’s atmosphere, with each generation generating more heat than the last. This heat is why datacenters consume so much power and water; they need it to stay cool during operation.

The amount of heat produced by a chip and the speed at which it dissipates are both influenced by the materials used to make it. Today’s materials are at their limit, and new materials can improve chips by orders of magnitude. However, discovering a new material and getting it into a fab takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars. Most ideas die in this valley of death, between a science experiment and a fab.

Autoresearch for the lab

AI agents compress months of inter-disciplinary scientific work to days. Over the 3 months of our Y Combinator batch, we simulated, synthesized and tested thermal interface materials that match the performance of products the world’s largest chemical companies have sold and guarded as trade secrets for over 20 years.

We’re also releasing Material Discovery Bench, an open-source benchmark for AI-driven materials discovery. We’ve built the benchmark in collaboration with experts from IBM, IMEC, Stanford and Cambridge, and it tests frontier model ability on a relevant, real-world materials problem. The benchmark has many verifiers for grading model ability, and we will continue building more in both simulation and experiment.

We’re building medical superintelligence.

We’re starting with medical and biological datasets, evaluations and reinforcement learning environments that help frontier labs train more capable, aligned and safe models.

What we offer

Off-the-shelf and custom datasets spanning patient histories, clinician–patient conversations, clinical reasoning and biological data. Our interactive environments let models gather information, use tools and work through multi-step medical tasks, with feedback on both clinical performance and behaviour.

Why medicine, why alignment

More capable models need to remain honest, reliable and responsive to human oversight in unfamiliar situations. Medicine is a perfect example of why this matters. Models must reason with incomplete information, recognise uncertainty, accept correction and avoid unsafe shortcuts. Strong benchmark scores alone don’t establish these behaviours.

We believe carefully designed medical and other beneficial data, environments and reward signals can improve clinical capability while helping aligned behaviours generalise beyond medicine. The literature shows this, and we’re building towards this across a broad range of models.

More varied data, fairer models

Models trained on a narrow slice of patients can perform unevenly across populations. We work with partners to build datasets spanning different people, conditions and care settings, including those underrepresented in existing data. Our aim is to make these gaps visible through evaluation and help models serve patients more fairly.

A continuous data flywheel

Our partnerships support ongoing clinical data collection and give us settings to deploy and evaluate models on real clinical tasks. New data and findings feed back into our datasets, training environments and separately released benchmarks. As models improve, the capability and safety gaps we uncover shape the next round of data and evaluations.

THE PROCESS

IN COLLABORATION WITH
ROSIE'S STORY
One breakthrough treatment later,

What we think

Every agent wants its own copy of every integration. You set up GitHub in Claude Code, then again in Cursor, then again in Codex. Same OAuth, same API key pasted in five places, and none of them agree on what a tool is allowed to do.

Your tools should belong to you, not to whichever agent you opened today. Executor turns everything into one shape: a name, an input, an output. An MCP server, an OpenAPI spec, and a GraphQL API all look the same to the agent, so you connect once and every agent gets it.

And the safe way has to be the easy way, or nobody does it. Executor knows a GET from a DELETE, asks before the scary ones, and runs everything in a sandbox where the model never sees a raw token.

Thousands of tools, one in the prompt

The model only ever sees one tool. Executor looks up what it needs when the code asks for it, so you can connect fifty services and the prompt stays the same size. Toggle a few below and watch the numbers.

EdotEnv's mission is to teach models recursive self-improvement. To get there, we build RL environments at scale from financial market data that increase in difficulty, so agents can continuously hillclimb.

01
WHY MARKETS
A frontier that keeps moving.

Recursive self-improvement is a loop: an agent researches, learns from the outcome, and returns to the next problem with better tools and judgment. The loop only continues when each round gets harder.

Markets create that pressure naturally. Every useful discovery attracts competition, and every successful strategy makes the next opportunity harder to find. Markets are a natural proving ground for agents that need to keep improving.

02
THE WORK
RL environments for harder problems.

We capture this dynamic in multi-step RL environments where agents form hypotheses, design experiments, verify results, and iterate. We use them to evaluate and post-train agents on increasingly difficult research tasks.

We work with frontier AI labs and academic groups building research harnesses, evaluation benchmarks, and post-training environments.

03
THE MISSION
Progress should belong to everyone.

We believe recursive self-improvement can help society reach scientific and technological breakthroughs faster—and make the benefits of that progress available regardless of socioeconomic status.

Our long-term goal is to redistribute the gains from faster progress equally to everyone.

visible_copy:
Skip to content
Waddle Labs
Writings
Waddle Labs

We are an applied AI lab building LLMs that control robots.

AI has advanced quickly, but robots still struggle outside carefully prepared settings. Making a robot useful often takes work specific to one machine, task, or lab. That makes progress difficult to reproduce and extend, and risks concentrating robot intelligence in a few large companies. We believe individuals should be able to adapt robots to their own needs. Our research aims to make that possible.

Model Capability. Language models are not perfect at robotics control, but they can learn in context. We have seen Waddle's agents become markedly more reliable over time. How do we preserve what one agent learns and transfer it to another? How do we build a shared memory across agents? Our work draws on and extends research in continual learning.
Inference Efficiency. We have shown that language models can solve robotics tasks in real time, on real robots, but latency remains a bottleneck. How can agents become faster with practice? How can we improve their efficiency while preserving the flexibility to adapt to new tasks and environments?
Human-robot interaction. Robot intelligence must be built for people. We study how people can give robots tasks, see what they are doing, and correct mistakes. We design interfaces that make it easy and safe for individuals to collaborate with robots.

If you are interested in working with us, please email founders@waddlelabs.ai.

For early access or other inquiries, please reach us via wave@waddlelabs.ai.

01

Traverse is a research lab that partners with frontier AI labs to produce the training data required for models to develop taste and judgment. Our work focuses on subjective and long-horizon tasks where success depends on reasoning, context, and decision-making. Our long-term goal is to give frontier models the foundations needed to perform and eventually surpass human white-collar work, accelerating the path toward artificial superintelligence.

02

Reinforcement learning recently produced superhuman models in domains like math and coding because these environments are largely deterministic. Most economically valuable work is not as deterministic; the work done in fields such as law, healthcare, sales, writing, and strategic decision-making is inherently ambiguous, where many outputs can be valid and quality depends on judgment, taste, and context. Training models to operate reliably in these environments remains one of the central unsolved problems in AI.

03

We believe non-deterministic work is fundamentally a context problem. Tasks that appear ambiguous become verifiable when enough information is captured about the situation, the constraints, and the reasoning behind expert decisions. Synthetic data produced by experts answering contrived prompts can help models perform adequately, but it cannot produce superhuman capability. What matters is observing real experts operating inside real environments and preserving the reasoning process that leads to their decisions. At scale, this creates training signals that allow models to learn how judgment actually works, and that class of data does not yet exist. We are the pioneers.

Synthetic Sciences is an AI research lab building infrastructure for scientific superintelligence. We are the creators of OpenScience, Ascent & FrontierML.

02

AI systems are already producing research-level advances in mathematics, with new AI-assisted discoveries appearing in rapid succession. Mathematics benefits from comparatively fast, abundant, and trustworthy verification.

The stakes extend far beyond mathematics. Autonomous ML research could accelerate recursive self-improvement, while discoveries across the physical sciences could transform entire industries.

However, across empirical sciences, verification faces fundamental tradeoffs among speed, cost, and fidelity. This makes long-horizon research difficult to evaluate, train, and improve reliably. We believe capability breakthroughs in these fields will come from the discovery of novel methods for data generation and verification, paired with algorithms designed around these constraints.

03

We are starting off by building reliable measures of scientific capability. We are developing high-fidelity, long-horizon evaluations that test whether models can form hypotheses, design and execute experiments, interpret failures, and make useful progress under uncertainty and resource constraints.

These evaluations are paired with inference-time scaffolding that provides realistic tools, persistent experimental state, and sufficient search budgets to isolate model failures.

hero_headlines: Transformative AI is here. Now what?
visible_copy:
Careers
Get in touch
Transformative AI is here. Now what?

Every transformative technology needed infrastructure to become exponential. The grid for electricity. CUDA for GPUs. AI needs its own, and its core is formal verification. And we are building that infrastructure.

Mathematics has already validated it. Mathlib, a library of formally verified knowledge built over years, is what lets models operate at the frontier of the field: this year they settled the Jacobian conjecture, open since 1939, and improved century-old bounds related to the Riemann hypothesis. Fermat’s Last Theorem - often cited as one of humanity’s greatest achievements - was recently autoformalized in a matter of days, outpacing collaborative human efforts that have been ongoing for years.

Software is next, and the stakes are higher. The same proofs for mathematical theorems can also prove software correct. Most production code is increasingly written by machines, faster than humans can review or test. At the same time, frontier AI is becoming increasingly capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. Under these conditions, proving correctness is now imperative.

As proofs hold for every input and are machine-checkable, correctness no longer depends on a human reading and reviewing code. And proven results never need to be checked again, so knowledge can compound - allowing us to build and control arbitrarily complex systems whose output exceeds human comprehension.

Just as Mathlib exponentiated math, we are building the infrastructure to exponentiate software. We are starting with one of the holy grails of computer science: verifying code down to the binary. And that is just one part of a larger infrastructure we are building.

It’s an exciting time to be alive.

WHY WE EXIST
Robotics has a data problem

AI has made enormous progress by scaling data. Language models learned to reason by training on the collected text of the internet. Vision models learned to see from billions of images. But robotics has nowhere near enough.

Most robot training data comes from teleoperation: a human remotely controls a robot while it records. This produces thousands of hours at best, collected in controlled lab settings with limited variety. Meanwhile, 8 billion people generate 16 hours of real-world physical activity every day. The gap is massive.

For robots to learn how the physical world works, they need to see how humans move through it. Not in a lab, but in real kitchens, offices, hotels, and homes. The messier and more diverse the data, the better the models.

That is what we do. We collect human activity data at scale from real environments across multiple continents, and turn it into clean, annotated datasets that teach robots to understand the physical world.

Klaus has shut down

Thank you for being part of Klaus. The service ended on September 1, 2026, and the web app and all customer assistants are now offline.

Billing: every subscription was cancelled before the shutdown. No further charges will be made.

Your data: the in-app export closed with the service. If you downloaded an export, it contains everything you need to move to a self-hosted assistant (see below). If you did not, email us and we will do what we can.

Where to go next

Klaus was built on OpenClaw, an open-source project we do not own. Because the software is free and open, you can keep running the same kind of assistant without us.

Run it yourself

Install OpenClaw on your own computer or a small cloud server using the install guide. If you have a Klaus export, it includes a recovery prompt: paste it into your new OpenClaw and it restores your workspace, skills, and chat history, then walks you through reconnecting channels like Slack, Telegram, and WhatsApp. A small always-on server runs roughly $5 to $12 a month, plus whatever you pay your AI provider for usage.

Moving between machines is covered at docs.openclaw.ai/install/migrating.

Use a managed host

If you would rather not run a server, KiloClaw is an independent company that hosts OpenClaw for you. We are not affiliated with them and cannot support them, so please review their current pricing and supported channels before you sign up.

Try Anthropic Cowork

If you are open to a different assistant altogether, Anthropic Cowork is Anthropic's own agentic workspace. It will not carry over your Klaus history, but it is a fully managed alternative.

Questions?

Email support@klausai.com.

© 2026 Usebits Inc

SKIP AHEAD
We have no shortage of new drugs being tested.
However composite success rates are very low.
But why?

Cancers are heterogenous and rapidly evolving. This makes it hard to determine who is likely to benefit from a drug at population scale.

20.6 million new cases and 10 million deaths every year.

Each one the result of evolution under the selective pressure of a unique environment: the tissue, the immune environment, metabolism, nutrients and more.

Most patients are unlikely to respond to a drug.

The variation that is characteristic of the disease warrants clearly identifying the patient profiles that will benefit from each medicine, ensuring higher success most critically in Phase 2.

Response could be predicted before enrollment.

Not after the trial reads out, but before it is designed.

How do we know who will respond?

DATA ENGINE

By mapping tumor biology using real patient tissue.

Every tumor we profile adds a datapoint capturing intra- and inter-tumoral heterogeneity. Computational analysis tools, biomarkers and deep learning systems can be used to model and generalize this distribution of malignant tissue. Underlying it is high-signal data, at scale.

The bottleneck

On any given day, ten people orbit Earth at 28,000 kilometers per hour, four hundred kilometers overhead. A feat of engineering that was science fiction for nearly all of human history is now routine.

Astronaut time is valued at $130,000 an hour [1]. Almost all of that cost goes to the systems that keep them alive, while the science occurs in the margins [2]. For the first time in history, the bottleneck in orbit is not rockets or science, but labor.

General Astronautics will build and scale orbital manufacturing factories, starting with industrial robotics. We are decoupling humanity's ambition and reach from the scarcity of astronaut time.

The ambition of our time: a colony on Mars, a sustained presence among the stars, new industries in computing, in resource extraction, in power. Every future of this kind runs through the same gate. There is more work than there are hands.

The future of orbit is industrial. Private stations need cargo logistics, experiments tended, components repaired, and structures inspected. Spacewalks are the most dangerous work an astronaut performs, and most of them should not have to happen at all. Orbital datacenters need GPUs replaced and modules upgraded across years of uptime. Satellites need refueling, repair, and eventual deorbit.

Then the Moon. We need habitats assembled, regolith shielding laid, power installed, comms deployed. The first permanent lunar presence is a construction site, not a crew.

Then Mars. The same work, with six months of resupply lag and inherent communications delay. Robots must build the infrastructure for human arrival.

This is how humanity becomes interplanetary. A ship that needs a crew to maintain itself for a century is a ship nobody builds. A ship that maintains itself is a ship that can actually be launched. That ship is on the horizon. The work begins today.
